newsitem.title: USA: Ekco closes two U.S. plants, stock tumbles.
newsitem.headline: Ekco closes two U.S. plants, stock tumbles.

text.p: Housewares maker Ekco Group Inc. said Wednesday it will close two plants and warned of quarterly and full-year losses, sparking a 24 percent drop in the value of its stock.
Ekco fell 75 cents to $4 on the New York Stock Exchange.

The company, which manufacturers kitchenware, plastic storage products, brooms, brushes and mops, predicted a loss of $22 million, or $1.18 a share, in the third quarter and a loss for the year of $29 million, or $1.53 a share.
For all of 1995, Ekco earned $8 million, or 40 cents a share, on revenues of $278 million.
The Nashua, N.H.-based company blamed the downturn on special charges and lower-than-expected sales.
Ekco also announced it will close plants in both East Hampston, Mass., and Hamilton, Ohio, transfering 200 jobs to its Obregon, Mexico, plant.
Local labour officials blasted the move saying it reflected an eagerness among manufacturers to take advance of less expensive labour under the North American Free Trade Agreement.

Louis Leopold, former secretary/treasurer of Massachusett's central labour council, AFL-CIO, said, "This is a direct result of NAFTA. Basically what's happening in the blue-collar industries is they're saying, why pay $7 or $8 an hour when you can pay $2 an hour in Mexico?"

Ekco said its plastics business has been under severe price and cost pressures for the past several years. It said it has not been able to recover higher resin costs through increased prices and has been forced to offer larger discounts on many products to remain competitive in the marketplace.
Ekco expects to announce its latest results during the week of Oct. 21.
The company also said its board of directors suspended the payment of a quarterly dividend and does not anticipate paying cash dividends for the foreseeable future.
Ekco Treasurer John Haran said, "We regret the loss of jobs at the existing plants. The cost to manufacture products at these locations has not been competitive."
The Easthampton, Mass., plant employs 220 people in three shifts and makes househouse brushes. The Hamilton, Ohio plant employs 70 people and makes long-handled brooms and mops.
